title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
summary: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

title: Measuring, Revealing and Mitigating Harmful Content Propagation in Recommender Systems
summary: Recommender systems help users navigate vast amounts of information by filtering content according to their historical behaviors. As these systems increasingly shape everyday information access, they largely determine the content users are exposed to. However, current research typically prioritizes catering to user interest, while overlooking the existence and propagation of harmful content, such as violence, hate speech, and pornography. In this work, we take a systematic step toward investigating harmful content in recommender systems from three aspects: measuring, revealing, and mitigating. First, we construct datasets with harmfulness-related annotations and present new evaluation metrics to quantitatively measure the harmfulness of recommendation results. Second, our empirical analysis reveals that users tend to engage with harmful content and prevailing recommendation methods often contribute to the proliferation of such content. Third, to address this issue, we introduce a generic framework, MitiHarm, which integrates harmfulness-related signals into both item and user representation learning. Experiments show that MitiHarm can significantly mitigate the propagation of harmful content while preserving user satisfaction. Resources of this work are available at https://github.com/Zhang-xiaokun/MitiHarm.

title: Serving-Aligned Entire-Space Conversion Modeling via Click-Through Rate Knowledge Distillation
summary: Recommendation systems may use predicted click-through conversion rate (pCTCVR), the product of predicted click-through rate (pCTR) and post-click conversion rate (pCVR), to guide ranking decisions. Many pCVR models build on the Entire Space Multi-Task Model (ESMM), which jointly trains pCVR and auxiliary pCTR towers using pCTR and pCTCVR losses, but deploys only the pCVR tower. At serving time, this tower may be paired with a separately trained pCTR model, creating a training-serving mismatch in pCTCVR when its predictions differ from those of the auxiliary pCTR tower. In this paper, we use knowledge distillation (KD) from logged serving pCTR scores to supervise ESMM's auxiliary pCTR tower and improve training-serving pCTCVR alignment. We denote variants by KD-$α$, where $α$ controls the hard-label loss weight. On the Ali-CCP dataset, KD-0.3, the best variant on serving pCTCVR, increases ROC-AUC not only for serving pCTCVR but also for pCVR by 2.1% and 1.6%, respectively, and PR-AUC by 9.9% and 8.8%, respectively, relative to the ESMM baseline. We also test negative downsampling with 5% nonclick retention. Downsampled KD-0.3 increases mean AUC for serving pCTCVR and pCVR by 1.2% and 0.9%, respectively, -and PR-AUC by 8.5% and 4.5%, respectively, relative to downsampled ESMM.

title: UMER: Unifying Embedding and Ranking via Pair-Aware Discriminative Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Modern Web information access increasingly involves heterogeneous multimodal content, including images, videos and visually rich documents. Users may seek not only globally similar content but also candidates that satisfy fine-grained attributes, relations or answer evidence under complex instructions. Supporting such access requires both efficient corpus-scale retrieval and fine-grained relevance reasoning. Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based embedding methods derive representations from MLLM hidden states, and recent work further uses Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to improve embedding capability by injecting intermediate semantic evidence into the representation. However, existing CoT methods typically use item-wise reasoning over queries and candidates in isolation, providing no explicit evidence to distinguish a positive from a semantically confusable hard negative. Moreover, contrastive embeddings capture global similarity but struggle with meta-tasks requiring answer verification, category judgment or fine-grained reasoning. In this paper, we propose UMER, a Unified Multimodal Embedding and Ranking framework for universal multimodal retrieval. UMER replaces item-wise reflection with PairAware Discriminative Reasoning, which compares query-candidate pairs to identify instruction-relevant matching and discrepancy evidence. UMER jointly learns contrastive embeddings for efficient global matching and discriminative ranking for explicit pairwise relevance judgment within a single MLLM. A complementary mutual distillation strategy further transfers reliable pairwise preferences between the embedding and ranking functions. On MMEB-V2, UMER-R scores 65.5/70.6 with Qwen2-VL-2B/7B, outperforming the strongest included matched-backbone baselines by 1.4/2.0 points. UMER also supports budget-adjustable inference from efficient embedding retrieval to optional pair-aware reranking.

title: The Oracle and The Prism: A Decoupled and Efficient Framework for Generative Recommendation Explanation
summary:
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into explainable recommendation systems often leads to a performance-efficiency trade-off in end-to-end architectures, where joint optimization of ranking and explanation can result in suboptimal compromises. To resolve this, we propose Prism, a novel decoupled framework that rigorously separates the recommendation process into a dedicated ranking stage and an explanation generation stage. This decomposition ensures that each component is optimized for its specific objective, eliminating inherent conflicts in coupled models.
  Inspired by knowledge distillation, Prism leverages a powerful, instruction-following teacher LLM (FLAN-T5-XXL) as an Oracle to produce high-fidelity explanatory knowledge. A compact, fine-tuned student model (BART-Base), the Prism, then specializes in synthesizing this knowledge into personalized explanations. Our extensive experiments on benchmark datasets reveal a key finding: the distillation process not only transfers knowledge but also acts as a noise filter. Our 140M-parameter Prism model significantly outperforms its 11B-parameter teacher in human evaluations of faithfulness and personalization, demonstrating an emergent ability to correct hallucinations present in the teacher's outputs. While achieving a 24x speedup and a 10x reduction in memory consumption, our analysis validates that decoupling, coupled with targeted distillation, provides an efficient and effective pathway to high-quality, and perhaps more importantly, trustworthy explainable recommendation.

title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
summary: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including a large multilingual embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-8B, 0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment best predicts how BM25 responds to explanations, embedding proximity how dense encoders do. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known-item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open-weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal-match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what-the-query-remembers.

title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and Decision Models
summary: Multi-hop retrieval must find passages that become useful only after intermediate evidence is retrieved. We present SAG2, an embedding-free retriever whose only persistent structure is a SQLite lexical index, built without an LLM. Where SAG and HippoRAG 2 rely on a generative LLM for graph extraction and selection, SAG2 uses a decision model. Given the question and a shared context of selected retrieved passages, the decision model scores whether each candidate supplies an answer-chain fact. Terms activated from the top-scoring passages retrieve unvisited passages through the lexical index, which holds a passage-term hypergraph implicitly. SAG2 reaches Recall@10 of 86.62%, 97.43%, and 99.00% on 1,000-question subsets of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA, the highest among the compared systems. With a decision model priced at about a fifth of SAG's LLM, indexing and retrieval on MuSiQue cost USD 4.33 against USD 14.85 for SAG. On EnterpriseRAG-Bench, SAG2 reaches 81.12% document Recall@10. As the benchmark's nested corpus grows 447.5-fold, SAG2's Recall@5 lead over BM25 alone widens from 7.28 to 14.76 points, at a nearly constant model cost per question. Because indexing makes no model call, SAG2 suits corpora that change often or must be searchable as soon as they are indexed.

title: Parametric Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Latent Routing of LoRA Adapters
summary: Parametric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (PRAG) is a RAG approach that integrates external knowledge directly into model parameters using a LoRA adapter, aiming at reducing the inference cost compared to traditional RAG. However, current PRAG approaches adopt a \textit{one-to-one} document encoding scheme, using a dedicated LoRA adapter for each individual document. This scheme introduces two major limitations: 1) As the number of documents increases, there will be a prohibitive cost for training and storage. 2) The LoRA adapters may largely overlap due to the shared knowledge across documents, making the approach highly inefficient. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Poly-PRAG approach, which uses a small set of LoRA adapters that are able to encode more general knowledge. Each document can be encoded using a combination of them through a latent routing function. By jointly training the LoRA adapters and the latent routing function, each LoRA adapter is able to encode a shared part of the knowledge across documents, and the routing function can select the best combination of adapters for a document. Experimental results on four benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the Poly-PRAG compared to other strong PRAG baselines. In addition, this approach reduces the storage requirement by avoiding the need to store a large number of LoRA adapters and offers a more efficient way to encode external knowledge into LLMs.
